source.title: Analyzing (In)Abilities of SAEs via Formal Languages
source.authors: Abhinav Menon; Manish Shrivastava; David Krueger; E. Lubana

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure content is flattened, but Table 1 and the relevant text are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures model output validity when SAE reconstructions replace hidden activations. This bears on whether omitting the SAE error affects model behavior, but it does not use the original study's error-predictability measurements.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports validity of generations after SAE reconstructions replace activations, averaged over regularization values and hidden sizes. The feature-clamping experiments measure effects of selected SAE latents, not the SAE error term, so they are not included as rows. The hidden-size power-law result concerns aggregate reconstruction loss, not per-token error norms or whether larger SAEs fail on the same tokens.
record.test_reason: Table 1 splices SAE reconstructions into small formal-language transformers, which drops the SAE error term. It then measures the validity of the resulting generations against the clean model's >99%. This is a new setting with a direct result on whether discarding the error term costs model behaviour (V5). It has no random-error control (so V3 is untested) and no linear/nonlinear error decomposition.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs on formal-language models find interpretable latents, but results (including reconstruction validity) are highly sensitive to training choices. They find correlational features often lack causal effects and argue causality should be built into SAE training. Their causal-loss SAE gives predictable causal features for some English parts of speech, but is biased toward MLP-read features and can reduce grammaticality.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains conventional SAEs with L1 or top-k sparsity on formal-language model activations and studies reconstruction validity and feature interventions; it does not apply the original dark-matter error-predictability method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reconstruction validity varies substantially with regularization method and normalization/pre-bias architecture variant; Table 1 averages over regularization values and hidden sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-k SAE aggregate reconstruction MSE falls as a power law in hidden size (exponents -0.07 to -0.38) across four architecture settings (Fig. 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In formal-language transformers, aggregate top-k SAE reconstruction error decreases with dictionary size following a power law, without vanishing over 1x–8x.

fits_no_version.finding: The functional cost of reconstruction varies from total failure to none depending on sparsity method and normalization (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How much model behaviour is lost when SAE error is dropped depends strongly on SAE training choices (top-k vs L1, normalization, pre-bias).

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The experiments use simplified synthetic formal languages. Table 1 aggregates across regularization values and hidden sizes, reports no uncertainty, and measures grammatical validity rather than general model behavior. The clean-model reference is stated only as more than 99%. No matched random-error comparison is provided.
record.rows_left_out: Feature-clamping results in Sections 3.2 and 4 and Appendix D were omitted because they test selected feature interventions, not the SAE reconstruction error term. Figure 10's aggregate reconstruction-loss scaling is noted under fits_no_version because it does not report per-token error norms or same-context failures across SAE sizes.

untested.parts: No regression of SAE error on input activations.
No per-token error norms, no cross-size overlap of failing contexts. Only aggregate MSE power laws versus hidden size (Fig. 10).
No comparison with random errors of equal norm. Only validity under reconstruction.
No split into linear and nonlinear error components.
No circuit or steering analysis run with versus without the error term. The tested part is behaviour loss from whole-layer reconstruction, measured as grammatical validity.
Training choices are varied, but error size (dark-matter share) is not measured as a function of them, and end-to-end training is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its reconstruction-validity measure is a whole-layer splice, not a circuit/steering analysis, so V5 support is indirect. Table 1 averages hide per-SAE variation, and the averages include poorly trained SAEs. The feature-clamping experiments concern latents, not the error term, and were rightly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether a large share of SAE error is a linear function of the input activation.

The study reports aggregate reconstruction loss scaling with hidden size, but does not measure per-token error norms across SAE sizes, overlap in failing contexts, or whether error vanishes with scale.
It evaluates validity after SAE reconstruction, but does not compare model loss under reconstruction errors with random errors of the same size.
The study does not separate linear and nonlinear error components or test whether they correspond to unlearned features versus a distinct residual.
It measures grammatical validity after replacing activations with SAE reconstructions, not the effects on circuits or steering, nor a general share of model behavior.

The study varies SAE training choices and proposes a causal-loss objective, but does not test whether dark matter is mostly a training artifact or whether its size shrinks under better architectures or end-to-end training.

relationships.condition: L1 SAEs in all architectures, and top-k SAEs with architectures II and IV (plus Dyck/English under I/III), all languages
relationships.reason: Replacing activations with SAE reconstructions cuts validity from >99% to 0–69% (r1–r13, r16–r19, r21–r24), so dropping the error destroys behaviour.
relationships.display_finding: Across the cited settings, reconstruction reduced validity from above 99% to 0–80.79%; architecture-I top-k English retained 92.46% validity.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: L1 SAEs in all architectures, and top-k SAEs with architectures II and IV (plus Dyck/English under I/III), all languages
source_check.reason: The condition as written includes architecture-I top-k English, whose 92.46% validity is classified as partial in r15 and separately covered by l1. To retain supports for the cited rows, restrict architecture-I top-k to Dyck-2 and architecture-III top-k to Dyck-2/English. The cited reconstruction validities range from 0% to 80.79% (r21), not 0–69%.

relationships.condition: Top-k SAE, architecture I, English model
relationships.reason: Validity stays at 92.46% (r15), a small loss. The cost of dropping the error depends heavily on SAE training choices.
relationships.display_finding: Reconstruction retained 92.46% validity, showing relatively little behavioral loss in this training configuration.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Top-k SAE, architecture I, English model
source_check.reason: r15 retains 92.46% validity against a clean reference above 99%, a substantially smaller degradation than most tested settings.

relationships.condition: Top-k SAEs, architectures I and III, Expr model
relationships.reason: Validity under reconstruction is 99.88% and 99.76%, matching the clean model's >99% (r14, r20). No behaviour is lost without the error term.
relationships.display_finding: Reconstruction retained 99.88% and 99.76% validity for architectures I and III, respectively, matching the clean model's validity above 99%.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Top-k SAEs, architectures I and III, Expr model
source_check.reason: r14 and r20 retain 99.88% and 99.76% grammatical validity without the error term. These challenge a meaningful loss on this metric; the coarse clean reference above 99% does not establish exactly zero degradation or preservation of every behavior.

tranche.reason: Formal-language transformers provide a new setting measuring grammatical validity after replacing first-block activations with SAE reconstructions.

source_check.notes: Table 1 averages across widths and sparsity settings; Appendix C.2 restricts subsequent feature analysis to well-reconstructing SAEs.
